content: Domestic Violence Act, 2005 and Rules, 2006 | Detailed legal information Page 1 INDIAN WOMEN'S LEGAL RIGHTS | DETAILED GUIDE Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 and Rules, 2006 A detailed, practical explanation of rights, remedies, procedures, duties and prescribed forms Scope: This guide explains the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 (the Act) and the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Rules, 2006 (the Rules), together. It is written for women seeking safety, protection, residence, financial relief, custody-related relief, compensation, medical care, shelter and access to justice. Source note: The 2006 Rules portion has been prepared with reference to the 31-page scanned Rules PDF supplied with the request. The scan's text was read from the document images. The Act portion is a detailed plain-language explanation of the statutory framework. Where the scan reproduces older references to the IPC, CrPC and Evidence Act, those are identified as legacy references requiring current-law cross-check. General legal information only

. Where the scan reproduces older references to the IPC, CrPC and Evidence Act, those are identified as legacy references requiring current-law cross-check. General legal information only. This is not a substitute for the official Gazette text, current amendments, court orders or advice from a qualified lawyer. Domestic Violence Act, 2005 and Rules, 2006 | Detailed legal information Page 2 PART I. UNDERSTANDING THE ACT AND WHO IT PROTECTS 1. Purpose and commencement The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 is a central law intended to provide more effective protection of the rights of women who are victims of violence occurring within the family or a domestic relationship. It recognises that domestic violence is not limited to visible physical injury. It includes sexual abuse, verbal and emotional abuse, economic abuse and threats. The Act creates a system of protection officers, service providers, applications to a Magistrate and a range of civil protection and relief orders. The Act came into force on 26 October 2006. The Rules, 2006 were also brought into force on 26 October 2006

. The Act came into force on 26 October 2006. The Rules, 2006 were also brought into force on 26 October 2006. The Act and Rules must be read together: the Act establishes rights, remedies and institutional duties; the Rules describe how information, reports, applications, safety planning, counselling, notice service, shelter, medical assistance and breach reports are handled. 2. Who can seek relief? An 'aggrieved person' under the Act is a woman who is, or has been, in a domestic relationship with the respondent and alleges that she has been subjected to an act of domestic violence by that respondent. The Act's protection is therefore not restricted to a woman who is currently living with the respondent. The relationship and shared-household requirements in the definitions must, however, be established. A 'domestic relationship' means a relationship between two persons who live or have, at any point of time, lived together in a shared household, when they are related by consanguinity, marriage, a relationship in the nature of marriage, adoption, or are family members living together as a joint family

. The respondent definition and the meaning of shared household should be read with the full Act and binding court decisions. A child is a person below 18 years and includes an adopted, step or foster child. The Act's protections may therefore be relevant to children in the aggrieved woman's care and custody, including through custody and protection orders. Child sexual abuse may separately trigger POCSO. Important: The Act is not ordinarily a remedy for harassment by a stranger who has never been in a qualifying domestic relationship with the woman. Other criminal, workplace or civil laws may apply to such conduct. 3. Key definitions in Section 2  Aggrieved person: a woman in or formerly in a domestic relationship who alleges domestic violence by the respondent.  Domestic relationship: the specified family, marriage, marriage-like, adoption or joint-family relationship involving living together in a shared household, currently or at some earlier time.  Shared household: the household where the woman lives or at any stage has lived in a domestic relationship, alone or with the respondent

.  Shared household: the household where the woman lives or at any stage has lived in a domestic relationship, alone or with the respondent. Ownership or title in the woman's name is not a precondition to the statutory residence right; the exact scope is subject to the Act and judicial interpretation.  Domestic violence: has the meaning in Section 3 and includes physical, sexual, verbal/emotional and economic abuse, as well as threats.  Protection Officer: an officer appointed by the State Government to assist the Magistrate and aggrieved women in implementing the Act.  Service provider: an organisation registered under Section 10 to provide prescribed support such as legal, medical, financial, counselling or shelter-related assistance.  Respondent: the person against whom relief is sought, subject to the statutory definition and judicial interpretation. PART II. WHAT COUNTS AS DOMESTIC VIOLENCE 4

.  Respondent: the person against whom relief is sought, subject to the statutory definition and judicial interpretation. PART II. WHAT COUNTS AS DOMESTIC VIOLENCE 4. Section 3: the complete categories of domestic violence Section 3 provides that an act, omission or commission or conduct of the respondent constitutes domestic violence if it harms, injures or endangers, or tends to harm, injure or endanger, the health, safety, life, limb or well-being, whether mental or physical, of the aggrieved person. It includes physical abuse, sexual abuse, verbal and emotional abuse, and economic abuse. The section also covers harassment, harm, injury or endangerment intended to coerce the woman or a person related to her to meet an unlawful demand for dowry, property or valuable security. Threats of conduct falling within the categories are also covered. The section further includes conduct that otherwise causes physical or mental injury or harm. 5. Physical abuse Physical abuse includes conduct causing bodily pain, harm or danger to life, limb or health. The Act's explanation includes assault, criminal intimidation and criminal force

. 5. Physical abuse Physical abuse includes conduct causing bodily pain, harm or danger to life, limb or health. The Act's explanation includes assault, criminal intimidation and criminal force. Examples include beating, slapping, hitting, biting, kicking, punching, pushing, shoving, causing injury or preventing access to necessary medical treatment. Domestic Violence Act, 2005 and Rules, 2006 | Detailed legal information Page 3 A woman does not need to wait until an injury becomes severe before seeking protection. The legal question is whether the conduct falls within the Act's definition and whether the requested relief is justified on the material before the Magistrate. Where the conduct also discloses a criminal offence, a separate police complaint may be appropriate. 6. Sexual abuse Sexual abuse includes conduct of a sexual nature that abuses, humiliates, degrades or otherwise violates the dignity of a woman. The Rules' Form I and Form IV examples include forced sexual intercourse, forcing a woman to watch pornography or obscene material, forcibly using her to entertain others, child sexual abuse, and other acts of a sexual nature that abuse or humiliate her

. The domestic-violence remedy is not a substitute for criminal law. Depending on the facts, sexual violence may also engage BNS provisions, POCSO where a child is involved, and other applicable criminal statutes. Consent, age and the exact conduct matter. 7. Verbal and emotional abuse Verbal and emotional abuse includes insults, ridicule, humiliation, name-calling and accusations concerning a woman's character or conduct. The Act specifically includes insults for not having a male child, insults for not having a child, and insults for not bringing dowry. It also includes repeated threats to cause physical pain to a person in whom the woman is interested. The Rules' Form IV further gives examples such as preventing a woman or child in her custody from attending school or college; preventing her from taking up a job or forcing her to leave a job; preventing her or a child from leaving the house; preventing her from meeting people in the normal course; forcing her to marry against her will; preventing her from marrying a person of her choice; and forcing her to marry a person selected by others. 8

. 8. Economic abuse Economic abuse includes deprivation of financial or economic resources to which the aggrieved woman or her child is entitled under law, custom, court order or necessity. It includes household necessities, maintenance, rent, employment-related resources, property, stridhan and assets. Examples in the Act and Rules include not providing money for the woman or her children; withholding food, clothes or medicines; forcing her out of the home or preventing her from using part of it; obstructing her employment; refusing to pay rent in rented accommodation; preventing use of clothes or household articles; selling, pawning or disposing of stridhan or valuables without consent; forcibly taking her salary, income or wages; and refusing to pay bills such as electricity. Practical point: Economic abuse is not limited to a husband refusing to hand over cash. It may include controlling the woman's earnings, withholding basic necessities, taking jewellery, blocking access to a shared home, preventing employment, or disposing of property or stridhan. 9

. It may include controlling the woman's earnings, withholding basic necessities, taking jewellery, blocking access to a shared home, preventing employment, or disposing of property or stridhan. 9. Dowry-related harassment and threats Harassment to coerce a woman or a person related to her to meet an unlawful demand for dowry, property or valuable security is expressly covered. Threats to commit physical, sexual, verbal/emotional or economic abuse are also relevant. The Dowry Prohibition Act and applicable BNS provisions may create separate criminal consequences. Relief under the Domestic Violence Act can be pursued in parallel where its requirements are met. PART III. RIGHTS AND RELIEFS UNDER THE ACT 10. Section 17: right to reside in a shared household Every woman in a domestic relationship has the right to reside in the shared household, whether or not she has any right, title or beneficial interest in it. She cannot be evicted or excluded from the shared household or any part of it by the respondent except in accordance with procedure established by law. This is a right of residence, not an automatic transfer of ownership. The woman may seek a residence order under Section 19

. This is a right of residence, not an automatic transfer of ownership. The woman may seek a residence order under Section 19. The court must consider the statutory framework, the facts and applicable binding decisions. 11. Section 18: protection orders After giving the parties an opportunity to be heard and being prima facie satisfied that domestic violence has taken place or is likely to take place, the Magistrate may pass a protection order in favour of the aggrieved woman

. The order can prohibit the respondent from:  committing any act of domestic violence;  abetting or aiding the commission of domestic violence;  entering the place of employment of the woman or, if she is a child, her school or another place she frequents;  attempting to communicate with her in any form, including personal, oral, written, electronic or telephonic contact;  alienating assets, operating bank lockers or accounts, including stridhan or jointly held property, without permission of the Magistrate;  causing violence to dependants, relatives or persons who give the woman assistance against domestic violence; and Domestic Violence Act, 2005 and Rules, 2006 | Detailed legal information Page 4  committing any other act specified in the protection order. A protection order is tailored to the case. The woman should explain the conduct, the safety risk, the places where protection is needed, and the forms of contact or interference that should be prohibited. 12. Section 19: residence orders When disposing of an application under Section 12, the Magistrate may pass a residence order if satisfied that domestic violence has taken place

. 12. Section 19: residence orders When disposing of an application under Section 12, the Magistrate may pass a residence order if satisfied that domestic violence has taken place. The court may restrain the respondent from dispossessing or disturbing the woman's possession of the shared household; direct the respondent to remove himself from the shared household in appropriate circumstances; restrain the respondent or relatives from entering a portion of the household where the woman resides; restrain alienation or disposal of the shared household; restrain renunciation of rights in the shared household; or secure alternate accommodation of the same level or payment of rent. The court may also direct return of stridhan or other property or valuables to which the woman is entitled. The Act places limits on certain orders, including the statutory restriction on directing a woman to remove herself from the shared household. The court considers the circumstances and the legal requirements. 13

. The court considers the circumstances and the legal requirements. 13. Section 20: monetary relief The Magistrate may direct the respondent to pay monetary relief to meet expenses and losses suffered by the aggrieved woman and any child as a result of domestic violence. It may include loss of earnings; medical expenses; loss caused by destruction, damage or removal of property; and maintenance for the woman and her children, including maintenance in addition to or along with maintenance under other laws. The relief should be adequate, fair and reasonable and consistent with the standard of living to which the woman is accustomed. It may be ordered as a lump sum or monthly payment. If the respondent fails to pay, the Magistrate may direct the employer or debtor of the respondent to pay a portion of wages, salary or debt directly to the woman or into court, as the Act provides. 14. Section 21: custody orders The Magistrate may, at any stage of the hearing, grant temporary custody of a child or children to the aggrieved woman or a person applying on her behalf. The Magistrate may specify visitation arrangements. If visitation may be harmful to the child, the Magistrate may refuse it

. The Magistrate may specify visitation arrangements. If visitation may be harmful to the child, the Magistrate may refuse it. This is a temporary protective power and must be considered with the child's welfare and any other relevant family-court proceedings. 15. Section 22: compensation orders In addition to other reliefs, the Magistrate may direct the respondent to pay compensation and damages for injuries, including mental torture and emotional distress, caused by acts of domestic violence. A woman should describe the impact on her health, dignity, work, finances, family life and emotional well-being, and provide available supporting material. 16. Section 23: interim and ex parte orders The Magistrate may pass interim orders that are just and proper. If the Magistrate is satisfied that an application prima facie discloses that the respondent is committing, has committed or is likely to commit domestic violence, the court may grant an ex parte order on the basis of the woman's affidavit. Such order may include relief under Sections 18, 19, 20, 21 or 22. The Rules prescribe the affidavit format for an ex parte application

. Such order may include relief under Sections 18, 19, 20, 21 or 22. The Rules prescribe the affidavit format for an ex parte application. The woman should explain why immediate relief is required, what harm may occur if the court waits, the threats or previous incidents, and what specific interim orders are requested. 17. Other rights and related provisions  Section 24: the Magistrate must give free copies of the order to the parties, the police officer in charge of the police station within whose jurisdiction the court is situated, and the service provider, where applicable.  Section 25: a protection order remains in force until the aggrieved person applies for discharge. A party may seek alteration, modification or revocation if circumstances change; the court must record reasons and follow the statutory process.  Section 26: relief under Sections 18–22 may also be sought in legal proceedings before a civil, family or criminal court, in addition to other reliefs available under those proceedings. A woman must disclose relevant relief already sought or obtained

. A woman must disclose relevant relief already sought or obtained.  Section 27: jurisdiction may lie with the Judicial Magistrate First Class or Metropolitan Magistrate within whose local limits the aggrieved person permanently or temporarily resides, carries on business or is employed, the respondent resides or carries on business or is employed, or the cause of action arose.  Section 28: proceedings under Sections 12, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22 and 23 are governed by the prescribed procedure. The court may lay down its own procedure for disposal of an application under Section 12 or an ex parte application under Section 23(2), within the Act.  Section 29: an appeal lies to the Court of Session within 30 days from the date on which the Magistrate's order is served on the aggrieved person or respondent, whichever is later.  Section 30: Protection Officers and members of service providers are deemed public servants when acting or purporting to act under the Act

.  Section 30: Protection Officers and members of service providers are deemed public servants when acting or purporting to act under the Act. Domestic Violence Act, 2005 and Rules, 2006 | Detailed legal information Page 5  Section 31: breach of a protection order or interim protection order by the respondent is an offence punishable with imprisonment up to one year, or fine up to ■20,000, or both.  Section 32: the offence under Section 31 is cognizable and non-bailable. The court may conclude the offence on the sole testimony of the aggrieved person, as provided by the section.  Section 33: a Protection Officer who fails or refuses to discharge duties imposed by the Magistrate without sufficient cause may be punished with imprisonment up to one year, or fine up to ■20,000, or both, subject to the Act.  Section 34: cognizance of an offence under Section 33 is subject to the statutory complaint requirement.  Sections 35–37: provide protection for actions done in good faith, clarify that the Act is in addition to other laws, and empower the Central Government to make rules. PART IV. THE PROTECTION OF WOMEN FROM DOMESTIC VIOLENCE RULES, 2006 The Rules operationalise the Act

. PART IV. THE PROTECTION OF WOMEN FROM DOMESTIC VIOLENCE RULES, 2006 The Rules operationalise the Act. They explain how information reaches a Protection Officer, how a Domestic Incident Report is prepared, how an application and affidavit are made, how a Protection Officer supports the woman, what happens in emergencies, how service providers and counsellors are handled, how notices are served, how breaches are reported, and how shelter and medical facilities are accessed. 18. Rule 1: short title and commencement The Rules are called the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Rules, 2006. They came into force on 26 October 2006. 19. Rule 2: definitions The Rules define 'Act' as the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005; 'complaint' as an allegation made orally or in writing by any person to the Protection Officer; 'Counsellor' as a member of a service provider competent to give counselling under Section 14; 'Form' as a form appended to the Rules; and 'section' as a section of the Act. Expressions not defined in the Rules but defined in the Act carry the meanings assigned by the Act. 20

. Expressions not defined in the Rules but defined in the Act carry the meanings assigned by the Act. 20. Rule 3: qualifications and experience of Protection Officers Protection Officers appointed by the State Government may be government officers or members of non-governmental organisations, with preference to women. Every Protection Officer must have at least three years' experience in the social sector. The tenure must be a minimum of three years. The State Government must provide necessary office assistance so that the officer can perform statutory functions. 21. Rule 4: information to Protection Officers Any person who has reason to believe that domestic violence has been, is being, or is likely to be committed may give information to the Protection Officer having jurisdiction. Information may be oral or written. If given orally, the Protection Officer must reduce it to writing and obtain the informant's signature. If the informant cannot furnish a written statement, the officer must satisfy themselves about the informant's identity and keep a record. A copy of the recorded information must be given to the informant immediately and free of cost. 22

. A copy of the recorded information must be given to the informant immediately and free of cost. 22. Rule 5: Domestic Incident Report On receiving a complaint, the Protection Officer prepares a Domestic Incident Report (DIR) in Form I and submits it to the Magistrate. Copies are forwarded to the officer in charge of the police station within whose local limits the alleged violence took place and to service providers in that area. At the aggrieved woman's request, a service provider may also record a DIR in Form I and forward it to the Magistrate and Protection Officer having jurisdiction. A DIR records the woman's details, respondents and relationships, children, incidents by date/place/time, types of violence, supporting documents, orders requested and assistance needed. It is a structured record of allegations and requested protection, not a judicial finding that the allegations have been proved. 23. Rules 6 and 7: application and affidavit An application under Section 12 is to be made in Form II or as nearly as possible to it. The woman may ask the Protection Officer to help prepare and forward it to the Magistrate

. The woman may ask the Protection Officer to help prepare and forward it to the Magistrate. If she is illiterate, the Protection Officer must read the application to her and explain its contents. The affidavit required for an ex parte order under Section 23(2) is to be made in Form III. The supplied Rules document contains a form for the application and a separate affidavit. The application form allows the woman to identify which reliefs she seeks: protection, residence, monetary relief, custody, compensation and interim orders. It also asks for information about previous litigation and maintenance proceedings so that the Magistrate can understand the procedural background. 24. Rule 8: duties and functions of Protection Officers Domestic Violence Act, 2005 and Rules, 2006 | Detailed legal information Page 6 The Rules require the Protection Officer to assist the woman in making a complaint if she wishes; provide information about her rights in English or a local language using Form IV; assist with applications under Section 12, Section 23(2) and other provisions; and prepare a Safety Plan in consultation with her after assessing the dangers involved

. The officer must facilitate legal aid through the State Legal Aid Services Authority; help the woman and any child obtain medical aid and transport; help arrange transport to shelter; inform registered service providers that their services may be required; invite and scrutinise counsellor applications; maintain and periodically revise the list of counsellors; maintain records and copies of reports and documents; help prevent victimisation or pressure after reporting; liaise between the woman, police and service providers; and maintain records of service providers, medical facilities and shelter homes in the area. The Rules further require the Protection Officer to protect the aggrieved woman and take reasonable measures to prevent recurrence of domestic violence. 25. Rule 9: emergency action If a Protection Officer or service provider receives reliable information by email, telephone or similar means from the woman or another person that domestic violence is occurring or is likely to occur in an emergency, the officer or provider must seek immediate police assistance

. The police are to accompany them to the place of occurrence, record the Domestic Incident Report and present it to the Magistrate without delay for appropriate orders. 26. Rule 10: additional duties when directed by the Magistrate When directed in writing by the Magistrate, the Protection Officer may be required to visit the shared household and make a preliminary enquiry to clarify matters relevant to ex parte interim relief; report on the respondent's emoluments, assets, bank accounts or other documents; help restore the woman's personal effects, gifts and jewellery; assist her to regain custody of children or secure court-directed visitation; help enforce orders under Sections 12, 18, 19, 20, 21 or 23; and obtain police assistance to confiscate a weapon involved in the alleged violence. The officer may also perform other duties assigned by the State Government or Magistrate. 27

. The officer may also perform other duties assigned by the State Government or Magistrate. 27. Rule 11: registration and eligibility of service providers A voluntary association registered under the Societies Registration Act, a company registered under company law, or another legally recognised organisation whose objectives include protecting women's rights and providing lawful assistance may apply to the State Government for registration as a service provider in the prescribed form. The State Government may make enquiries and must satisfy itself about the applicant's suitability. An application should not be rejected without giving the applicant an opportunity to be heard. The Rules require the organisation to have rendered the type of services it proposes to provide for at least three years. Medical facilities, psychiatric counselling centres and vocational training institutions must meet the requirements of their relevant regulators. A proposed shelter home is subject to inspection, including assessment of capacity, safety and communication facilities. The State Government must provide and publish lists of service providers, and Protection Officers must maintain proper records

. The State Government must provide and publish lists of service providers, and Protection Officers must maintain proper records. 28. Rule 12: service of notices Notices for appearance must identify the person alleged to have committed domestic violence, the nature of the alleged violence and details that help identify the person. Notices are served by the Protection Officer or a person authorised by the officer at the address where the respondent is said to reside or be gainfully employed. The Rules describe delivery to a person in charge at the place and, where delivery is not possible, affixing the notice conspicuously. The Rules refer to the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 and the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 for service methods as far as practicable. They also permit the court to direct additional steps to expedite proceedings. Once service is reported, the court may deal with pending interim applications after hearing the relevant party or parties. The Rules clarify that where a protection order restrains entry, contact or approach, the woman's invitation or other conduct does not by itself waive the restraint

. The Rules clarify that where a protection order restrains entry, contact or approach, the woman's invitation or other conduct does not by itself waive the restraint. The court order remains effective unless duly modified under Section 25(2). 29. Rules 13 and 14: appointment and work of counsellors A counsellor is appointed from the list forwarded by the Protection Officer, with notice to the aggrieved woman. A person connected with the dispute or related to a party should not be appointed unless all parties waive the objection in writing. A lawyer who has appeared for the respondent in the case or connected proceedings is also ineligible. Counsellors should, as far as possible, be women. Counselling takes place under the general supervision of the court or Protection Officer at a place convenient to the woman or both parties. Its purpose is to understand the woman's grievances and identify measures to end domestic violence. The Rules state that the respondent should give an undertaking to refrain from further violence and, where appropriate, not to meet or contact the woman except through the counselling process or as permitted by law or court order

. The Rules prohibit the respondent from using counselling to justify the alleged violence. If the woman desires, the counsellor may attempt settlement, but the limited purpose is redress of her grievances and ending recurrence. The counsellor reports to the Magistrate. If settlement is reached, its terms are recorded and endorsed; the court may accept them after enquiry and reasons. If no settlement is reached, the counsellor reports failure and the court proceeds under the Act. The counselling record alone is not to be treated as the sole basis for an inference or order. Any order modifying or discharging protection must not be based on force, fraud or Domestic Violence Act, 2005 and Rules, 2006 | Detailed legal information Page 7 coercion. Safety and consent: Counselling is not a condition that a woman must accept before seeking legal protection. The Rules contemplate settlement efforts if the aggrieved person desires them. A woman facing danger should prioritise safety and legal protection, and should not be pressured into reconciliation. 30

. A woman facing danger should prioritise safety and legal protection, and should not be pressured into reconciliation. 30. Rule 15: reporting breach of protection orders A woman may report breach of a protection order or interim protection order to the Protection Officer in writing and sign the report. The Protection Officer forwards the complaint with a copy of the breached order to the Magistrate. The woman may instead complain directly to the Magistrate or police. If she needs assistance after a breach, the Protection Officer must immediately seek help from the local police station, assist in rescuing her where necessary and help lodge a report. Resistance to enforcement by the respondent or a person acting on the respondent's behalf is treated by the Rules as a breach. The Rules direct that breach be reported immediately to the police station with territorial jurisdiction and dealt with as a cognizable offence under Sections 31 and 32

. The Rules direct that breach be reported immediately to the police station with territorial jurisdiction and dealt with as a cognizable offence under Sections 31 and 32. The Rules also describe protective bail conditions that may be imposed, including no threats or violence, no harassment or contact, staying away from the woman's residence or places she is likely to visit, restrictions on firearms or dangerous weapons, restrictions on alcohol or drugs, and other conditions needed for safety and adequate relief. 31. Rule 16: shelter At the woman's request, the Protection Officer or service provider may make a written request to the person in charge of a shelter home under Section 6. If the Protection Officer makes the request, it should be accompanied by the Domestic Incident Report. However, a shelter home must not refuse shelter merely because the woman has not already lodged a DIR. If the woman wishes, the shelter home must not disclose her identity or communicate it to the person complained against. 32. Rule 17: medical facilities The woman, Protection Officer or service provider may make a written request to a medical facility under Section 7

. 32. Rule 17: medical facilities The woman, Protection Officer or service provider may make a written request to a medical facility under Section 7. If the Protection Officer makes the request, it should be accompanied by a DIR. A medical facility must not refuse medical assistance because a DIR has not been lodged beforehand. If no DIR exists, the medical facility must fill Form I and forward it to the local Protection Officer. The medical facility must provide the woman a copy of the medical examination report free of cost. PART V. FORMS IN THE 2006 RULES AND HOW THEY HELP 33. Form I: Domestic Incident Report Form I records the complainant/aggrieved woman's name, age, shared-household and current address and phone number; respondents and their relationship to her; children and where they are living; and each incident's date, place, time, alleged perpetrator and type of violence. It provides checklists for physical, sexual, verbal/emotional and economic violence, dowry-related harassment and other relevant information. It also records documents attached, the orders sought and assistance required. The form includes a section for police instructions

. It also records documents attached, the orders sought and assistance required. The form includes a section for police instructions. Where the information discloses an offence under criminal law, the police officer should inform the woman that she may initiate criminal proceedings by lodging an FIR. If she does not wish to initiate criminal proceedings at that time, the form describes recording the information and her stated preference to pursue civil protection remedies. If she reports physical injury or pain, immediate medical assistance and medical examination should be offered. 34. Form II: application to the Magistrate The application form allows the aggrieved woman, Protection Officer or another person on her behalf to apply to the Magistrate. It asks for the reliefs requested under Sections 18 to 22 and interim orders. The form contains categories for protection orders, residence orders, monetary relief, child custody and compensation. It also seeks details of previous litigation or maintenance proceedings so the court can consider related cases and orders. 35

. It also seeks details of previous litigation or maintenance proceedings so the court can consider related cases and orders. 35. Form III: affidavit for ex parte relief The affidavit supports an application for an urgent ex parte order under Section 23(2). The supplied form asks the applicant to identify herself, her relationship and shared household with the respondent, the application and reliefs sought, the history of living with the respondent, the facts supporting the application, her apprehension that violence may recur, the threats made, and why relief is urgent. It includes verification that the contents are true to the applicant's knowledge and belief. 36. Form IV: information on rights Form IV is a rights-information document intended to explain the Act in English or a local language. The supplied version describes examples of physical, sexual, verbal/emotional and economic violence and informs women that they can seek protection and assistance. It is designed to make rights understandable, not merely to collect facts. 37

. It is designed to make rights understandable, not merely to collect facts. 37. Form V and service-provider registration form Domestic Violence Act, 2005 and Rules, 2006 | Detailed legal information Page 8 Rule 8 refers to a Safety Plan in Form V, prepared in consultation with the woman after assessing dangers and considering an application under Section 12. A safety plan is a practical set of steps to reduce risk and prevent further violence. Rule 11 requires an organisation seeking registration as a service provider to apply in the prescribed form and satisfy eligibility and suitability requirements. The Rules should be read with the actual appended forms. The supplied scan includes the Domestic Incident Report, application, affidavit and rights information forms. Form labels and layout should be checked against the official Gazette copy before using them as blank templates in an actual proceeding. PART VI. HOW A WOMAN CAN USE THESE PROTECTIONS 38. Step-by-step pathway  Immediate safety first. If there is immediate danger, move to a safer place if possible and contact local police/emergency services. Do not delay urgent medical care or shelter while waiting to complete a form

. If there is immediate danger, move to a safer place if possible and contact local police/emergency services. Do not delay urgent medical care or shelter while waiting to complete a form.  Contact a Protection Officer or registered service provider. Explain the incidents and ask for information about the Act, assistance with a DIR, safety planning, legal aid, medical help and shelter.  Ask for the Domestic Incident Report. Provide a factual chronology: dates, places, conduct, people involved, children affected, injuries, financial deprivation, threats and supporting documents. Ask for a copy.  Seek the appropriate Magistrate's orders. An application under Section 12 can request protection, residence, monetary, custody and compensation relief. If urgent, ask about interim or ex parte relief under Section 23 and the affidavit.  Use parallel criminal remedies where applicable. If conduct discloses a criminal offence, a police complaint/FIR may be appropriate. Relief under the Domestic Violence Act is additional to other legal remedies.  Report any breach immediately. Give the Protection Officer, Magistrate or police a copy of the protection order and details of each breach

.  Report any breach immediately. Give the Protection Officer, Magistrate or police a copy of the protection order and details of each breach. Ask for immediate safety assistance.  Keep copies and track dates. Keep the DIR, application, affidavit, court orders, medical records, complaint acknowledgements and evidence in a safe place. 39. Evidence and records  Write a dated incident chronology with the location, what occurred, who was present, injuries, threats and any immediate action taken.  Preserve messages, emails, call logs, voice messages, photographs of injuries or damaged property, bank records, salary records, rent demands, medical prescriptions and bills.  Keep records showing ownership or possession of stridhan, jewellery, gifts, personal documents and household property, where available.  Identify witnesses, neighbours, relatives, colleagues, health workers or service providers who may have relevant information.  Keep copies of prior police complaints, DIRs, court applications, interim orders, protection orders and any breach reports.  Do not put yourself at risk to collect evidence

.  Keep copies of prior police complaints, DIRs, court applications, interim orders, protection orders and any breach reports.  Do not put yourself at risk to collect evidence. Do not hack accounts, trespass, threaten the respondent or circulate private material. 40. What reliefs can be requested together? A woman may seek more than one form of relief where the facts support it. For example, she may seek a protection order against threats and contact, a residence order to prevent dispossession, monetary relief for maintenance and medical expenses, temporary custody arrangements, and compensation for mental torture and emotional distress. The Magistrate decides what is justified under the Act. Relief under this Act may also be sought alongside appropriate proceedings under other laws, subject to disclosure and avoidance of inconsistent orders. 41. If the respondent violates the order A protection order is not merely advice. Section 31 makes breach of a protection order or interim protection order an offence. Under Rule 15, the woman can report the breach to the Protection Officer, Magistrate or police
